title: GraphQL N+1: DataLoader, Caching & Cost Limits
summary: A dense field guide to the GraphQL N+1 problem — why resolver-per-field execution explodes into hundreds of database round trips, how DataLoader batches and caches them away, and how query cost limits stop hostile or accidental queries before they run.

chapters.title: Why GraphQL Explodes: The N+1 Problem
points: Definition: N+1 = 1 query fetches N parents, then N extra queries fetch each parent's child — total N+1 round trips instead of 2
GraphQL executes per-field, not per-query: every field gets its own resolver invocation, so nesting multiplies calls
Concrete shape: `{ posts(first:50) { author { name } } }` = 1 query for posts + 50 queries for authors = 51 round trips
REST hides this behind hand-written endpoints; GraphQL exposes it because clients pick the shape at runtime
The server author cannot pre-optimize: the join set is unknown until the query arrives
Nesting compounds: posts → author → company → employees is 1 + 50 + 50 + 50N; depth multiplies, it does not add
Latency math: 51 queries × 8ms round trip = 408ms of pure network wait, even if each query is a 0.2ms indexed lookup
The database is usually not the bottleneck — round-trip count is; the same rows fetched in one `IN` query take ~10ms
Duplicate work is common: 50 posts by 5 authors still issues 50 author queries without deduplication
N+1 is not GraphQL-specific — ORMs (ActiveRecord, Hibernate lazy loading, Django) have the same failure — but GraphQL makes it the default
Symptom in logs: hundreds of identical `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?` lines with different ids, same request id
Why naive fixes fail: eager-loading everything wastes work when the client didn't ask for the field
Cost is per-request and scales with page size: doubling `first:` doubles the query count linearly
Key insight to hold: the fix is not fewer resolvers — it is deferring and grouping the loads resolvers request

chapters.title: How Resolvers Actually Execute
points: Every field in a GraphQL schema has a resolver; unspecified fields get the default resolver `(parent) => parent[fieldName]`
Resolver signature: `(parent, args, context, info)` — parent is the resolved value one level up
Execution is depth-first over the query AST but breadth-parallel across sibling fields at the same level
List fields fan out: resolving `[Post]` of length 50 calls the child `author` resolver 50 separate times
Each of those 50 calls is independent — it has no visibility into its 49 siblings, which is exactly why naive code re-queries
Resolvers may return promises; the executor awaits them, so sibling resolvers all start before any completes
That parallel start is the batching window: all 50 `author` resolvers fire in the same tick of the event loop
`context` is constructed once per request and passed to every resolver — the natural home for per-request loaders
`info` carries the AST, the field path, and the return type — the basis for lookahead/projection optimizations
Trivial resolvers still cost: property access on an already-loaded parent is free, a network call is not
The executor gives no built-in coordination between resolvers — batching must be added by you or a library
Mental model: GraphQL execution is a tree walk where each node may perform I/O; DataLoader turns per-node I/O into per-level I/O
Common misread: 'my resolver only runs once' — it runs once per parent object, not once per query

chapters.title: DataLoader: The Batching Primitive
points: DataLoader is a per-request utility that coalesces individual `.load(key)` calls into one `batchLoadFn(keys)` call
Created by Facebook, ~400 lines, transport-agnostic — works with SQL, Redis, HTTP, gRPC, anything keyed
Constructor: `new DataLoader(keys => batchFn(keys), options)`
API surface: `load(key)`, `loadMany(keys)`, `clear(key)`, `clearAll()`, `prime(key, value)`
`load(key)` returns a Promise immediately and queues the key; nothing is fetched yet
Batch function contract: given `keys: K[]`, return `Promise<(V | Error)[]>` of the SAME length, in the SAME order
Order contract is the #1 source of bugs: `SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...)` returns rows in arbitrary order and omits misses
Correct batch function remaps results: build a `Map` by id, then `keys.map(k => map.get(k) ?? null)`
Missing keys must yield `null` or an `Error` in the slot — never silently shorten the array
Returning an `Error` instance in a slot rejects only that key's promise, leaving siblings resolved
Minimal example: 50 `.load(authorId)` calls become one `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (1..12)`
`loadMany` never rejects — it resolves to an array that may contain Error values, unlike `Promise.all`
DataLoader is not a data-fetching library; it wraps whatever fetch you already have
Rule of thumb: one loader per (entity, access pattern) pair — `userById`, `postsByAuthorId`, not one god loader

chapters.title: Inside the Batch: Ticks, Queues & Scheduling
points: Mechanism: `.load()` pushes {key, resolve, reject} onto a queue and schedules a dispatch if none is pending
Default scheduler is `process.nextTick` (Node) — dispatch happens after the current synchronous frame drains
This means every `.load()` made in the same tick lands in one batch; loads in a later tick form a new batch
Why it works with GraphQL: sibling resolvers all fire synchronously in the same tick before any await resolves
`batchScheduleFn` option overrides the scheduler, e.g. `fn => setTimeout(fn, 10)` to widen the window across ticks
`maxBatchSize` splits a large batch into chunks — essential when the DB has a parameter limit (Postgres ~65535, SQL Server 2100)
`batch: false` disables batching entirely, leaving only the cache — useful for debugging or single-key sources
Sequential awaits break batching: `for (const id of ids) await loader.load(id)` produces N batches of 1
Fix: `await Promise.all(ids.map(id => loader.load(id)))` so all loads queue in one tick
Deeper levels batch per level, not globally: level-2 loads dispatch after level-1 resolves, so depth D costs D batches
That is the win: D round trips instead of N^D
Await ordering trap: awaiting a non-loader promise between loads pushes later loads into a new tick and a new batch
Deduplication happens at queue time — two `.load(7)` calls in one tick share a single promise and a single key in the batch

chapters.title: Per-Request Caching: Identity & Lifetime
points: DataLoader's second job: a memoization cache keyed by `load()` key, checked before queueing
Cache hit returns the SAME promise object — repeated `.load(7)` anywhere in the request costs zero extra I/O
Solves the diamond problem: post.author and comment.author both resolving user 7 fetch it once
Scope is one request, by construction — create loaders inside the per-request context factory, never at module scope
Module-scope loader = cross-request cache = users see each other's data; this is a real security bug, not a style nit
Per-request lifetime also means no invalidation problem: the cache dies with the request
Keys are compared by `===` (strict identity) — object keys never hit unless you pass the same reference
`cacheKeyFn` normalizes composite keys: `key => JSON.stringify([key.tenantId, key.id])` or a stable string
`cache: false` disables memoization but keeps batching — right for mutations that must see fresh rows
`clear(key)` after a mutation forces a refetch of that entity later in the same request
`prime(key, value)` seeds the cache from data you already have, e.g. after a list query returns full user rows
`prime` is a no-op if the key exists; `clear(key).prime(key, v)` to force an overwrite
Errors are cached too — a rejected load stays rejected for the request unless you clear it in the batch function's catch
`cacheMap` option accepts a custom Map-like store — the hook for LRU or a shared cross-request cache (with the risks above)

chapters.title: Wiring DataLoader Into a Real Server
points: Build loaders in the server's context function: `context: ({req}) => ({ user: auth(req), loaders: createLoaders(db) })`
`createLoaders(db)` returns a fresh object of loaders per call — the factory is the whole pattern
Resolver becomes one line: `author: (post, _, {loaders}) => loaders.userById.load(post.authorId)`
One-to-many needs a different batch function: group rows by foreign key, return an array per key, `[]` for no matches
Example: `postsByAuthorId` runs `WHERE author_id IN (...)`, then buckets rows into a `Map<authorId, Post[]>`
Pass tenant/auth scope into the loader factory so batched SQL stays scoped — never batch across tenants
Authorization must be re-checked per key: a batch that fetches 50 rows can leak rows the viewer may not see
Prime the loader from list queries: after `SELECT * FROM users`, `users.forEach(u => loaders.userById.prime(u.id, u))`
Mutations: `clear(id)` the mutated entity so later reads in the same response see the new value
Federation/microservices: batch the downstream HTTP call too — a `POST /users/batch` endpoint beats 50 GETs
Testing: assert on the number of batch-function invocations, not just on returned data — that is the regression that matters
Instrument: log `keys.length` per batch call; a histogram stuck at 1 means batching is broken somewhere upstream
Subscriptions and long-lived operations need a loader per event, not per socket — otherwise the cache goes stale forever

chapters.title: Alternatives & Comparisons
points: DataLoader: batches by key, per-request cache, ORM-agnostic — but still one query per level and per entity type
JOIN-based / lookahead resolvers: read `info` to project the requested fields into a single SQL JOIN — 1 query total
Lookahead wins on round trips, loses on complexity: you hand-write projection logic and duplicate the schema shape
Row multiplication: a JOIN across two one-to-many edges returns N×M rows and inflates payload; DataLoader does not
Join Monster / Prisma / Hasura / PostGraphile compile the GraphQL AST to SQL automatically — least code, least control
Prisma's fluent API batches `findUnique` calls automatically, giving DataLoader-like behavior without the wiring
Eager loading everything (`include: {author: true}` always) over-fetches when the client omits the field
Batching at the HTTP layer (persisted queries, `@defer`) reduces client round trips but does nothing for server N+1
Caching layers (Redis, `@cacheControl`, CDN on persisted queries) cut repeat cost across requests; DataLoader only helps within one
Comparison row — round trips: naive N+1, DataLoader D (depth), JOIN/lookahead 1
Comparison row — code cost: naive lowest, DataLoader medium, compiled-SQL layer highest lock-in
Comparison row — cache reuse: naive none, DataLoader per-request, Redis cross-request with invalidation burden
Rule: DataLoader is the default because it is correct everywhere; add lookahead only for proven hot paths
They compose — use lookahead on the top-level list query and DataLoader for everything the projection missed

chapters.title: Query Cost Limits: Stopping the Blast Radius
points: Batching bounds round trips, not work: `{a{b{c{d{e}}}}}` with `first:100` at each level is still millions of rows
GraphQL's flexibility is a DoS surface — one small query string can request unbounded work
Depth limiting: reject queries nesting deeper than N (typical 7-12); cheapest control, catches recursive cycles
Cyclic schemas make unbounded depth trivial: `user { friends { user { friends ... } } }` repeated 20 times
Breadth/node limiting: cap total nodes = product of list sizes along each path
Complexity/cost analysis: assign each field a cost, multiply list fields by their `first`/`limit` argument, sum, compare to budget
Static analysis runs before execution — the query is rejected without touching the database
Cost formula shape: `cost(field) = fieldCost + multiplier × Σ cost(children)` where multiplier comes from pagination args
Require pagination arguments: a list field with no `first`/`last` has an unknown multiplier — treat as infinite or reject
Cost directives put the number in the schema: `@cost(complexity: 10)` on expensive fields like full-text search
Per-client budgets: give trusted internal clients a higher ceiling than public tokens
Rate limit on cost points consumed per minute, not on request count — 1 request can cost 10,000 points
Timeouts and query-level row caps as the backstop when static cost underestimates reality
Persisted/allowlisted queries are the strongest control: production clients may only send pre-registered documents, making arbitrary cost impossible
Also cap: aliases (same field 1000× under different aliases), introspection in production, and `@skip`/`@include` abuse
Always return the cost in the error so clients can self-correct: `{extensions: {cost: 5200, max: 1000}}`

chapters.title: Gotchas, Anti-Patterns & Debugging
points: Batch function returns wrong-length array — DataLoader throws; always remap through a `Map`, never return raw rows
Batch function returns rows in DB order — silently returns the wrong user for every key; the worst bug in this space
Module-scope loader — cross-request cache leak; loaders must be created per request
Sequential `await` in a loop — batching silently degrades to N queries of size 1 with no error
Loader created inside a resolver — a new loader per call, so no batching and no cache at all
Object keys without `cacheKeyFn` — every load misses the cache because `{id:1} !== {id:1}`
Batching across tenants — one `IN` query spanning tenants leaks data if the WHERE clause loses the scope
Caching authorization-dependent results by id alone — viewer A's permission-filtered result served to viewer B
Forgetting `clear()` after a mutation — the rest of the response shows stale pre-mutation values
Cached rejections — a transient error poisons every later load of that key in the request
`maxBatchSize` unset against a parameter-limited driver — a 5000-key batch blows up the SQL parameter cap
Debug technique: log every SQL statement with the request id; repeated identical statements = a missing loader
Debug technique: count batch invocations in tests; add an assertion so a refactor cannot silently reintroduce N+1
Apollo Studio / OpenTelemetry traces show resolver spans — a wall of thin parallel spans at one level is the N+1 signature
Watch p99 not p50: N+1 hides at small page sizes and appears only when a client asks for `first: 100`

chapters.title: Summary: The Complete Defense
points: Layer 1 — schema design: require pagination args, avoid gratuitous cycles, keep expensive fields explicit
Layer 2 — static limits: depth, node count, complexity budget, checked before execution touches I/O
Layer 3 — DataLoader: batching turns N queries into 1 per level; caching dedupes within the request
Layer 4 — targeted lookahead/JOINs on measured hot paths only
Layer 5 — cross-request caching (Redis, cache-control hints) for data that tolerates staleness
Layer 6 — runtime backstops: timeouts, row caps, cost-based rate limits, persisted query allowlists
Complexity recap: naive nesting is O(N^D) queries; DataLoader makes it O(D) queries; compiled SQL makes it O(1)
Rows fetched does not shrink with DataLoader — only round trips do; cost limits are what bound rows
Checklist: loaders in context factory, order-preserving batch functions, `Promise.all` not sequential await, `clear()` after mutations
Checklist: `cacheKeyFn` for composite keys, `maxBatchSize` for driver limits, tenant scope inside the loader factory
Checklist: authorization enforced per key, never assumed from the batch
Test discipline: assert batch-call counts, not just response shape — that is what regresses
Measure before optimizing: log SQL per request, look at p99 with realistic page sizes
One-line takeaway: batch and cache per request to make queries cheap, then cap cost so no query can be expensive anyway
